events/greek-autocephaly-1833/summary: In the newly independent Kingdom of Greece, the Bavarian regency of King Otto declared the church within the kingdom autocephalous (July 1833), governed by a Holy Synod on the Russian model. Constantinople, still under Ottoman rule, initially regarded the act as uncanonical but recognised the Church of Greece by a Tomos in 1850.
events/greek-autocephaly-1833/causes/1: The new state's unwillingness to leave its church under a patriarch resident in Ottoman Constantinople
events/greek-autocephaly-1833/causes/2: Regency adviser Georg von Maurer's state-church design
events/greek-autocephaly-1833/consequenc: Seventeen years of strained relations with the Ecumenical Patriarchate
Pattern of 'national' autocephaly copied across the Balkans
events/madagascar-persecution-1835/summa: Queen Ranavalona I banned Christianity, expelled LMS missionaries and executed many Malagasy believers, some thrown from the cliffs of Ampamarinana. The underground church grew; after her death the court converted (1869) and Protestantism became dominant in the highlands.
events/niger-expedition-1841/summary: A British expedition up the Niger to promote 'Christianity and commerce' and end the slave trade lost many Europeans to fever, but the Yoruba recaptive Samuel Ajayi Crowther's journal impressed the CMS, which had him ordained in London in 1843. Henry Venn's vision of self-governing African churches followed.
events/niger-expedition-1841/causes/0: Abolitionist strategy of Thomas Fowell Buxton
events/wesleyan-methodist-connection-184: Abolitionist Methodists form the Wesleyan Methodist Connection

Abolitionist ministers including Orange Scott and Luther Lee left the Methodist Episcopal Church, which tolerated slaveholding members and clergy, and organised the Wesleyan Methodist Connection at Utica in May 1843. They forbade slaveholding, rejected episcopacy and gave laity a larger role.
Methodist Episcopal Church compromise over slavery and suppression of abolitionist agitation
Revivalist and holiness concern for a pure church
Pressure contributed to the 1844 North–South division of the Methodist Episcopal Church
The Wesleyan Chapel at Seneca Falls hosted the 1848 Women's Rights Convention
Merged with the Pilgrim Holiness Church in 1968 to form the Wesleyan Church
events/disruption-of-1843/summary: On 18 May 1843 about a third of the ministers of the Church of Scotland, led by Thomas Chalmers, walked out of the General Assembly and formed the Free Church of Scotland, giving up their stipends and manses. They protested that civil courts and lay patrons were overriding the church's spiritual independence in appointing ministers.
events/disruption-of-1843/causes/0: Patronage Act of 1712 allowing patrons to present ministers
events/disruption-of-1843/causes/1: The 'Ten Years' Conflict' and court rulings against the Veto Act (1834)
events/disruption-of-1843/causes/2: Evangelical party's doctrine of the 'Crown Rights of the Redeemer'
events/disruption-of-1843/consequences/0: Free Church of Scotland and a vast church-building and school programme
events/disruption-of-1843/consequences/2: Reunions of 1900 (United Free Church) and 1929 (with the Church of Scotland)
events/disruption-of-1843/consequences/3: Church of Scotland Act 1921 recognising spiritual independence
events/great-disappointment-1844/summary: Followers of the Baptist preacher William Miller expected Christ's return on 22 October 1844 based on calculations from Daniel 8:14. When it did not happen, the movement fragmented; one group reinterpreted the date as Christ entering the heavenly sanctuary and, with Ellen G. White, formed the Seventh-day Adventist Church (1863).
events/great-disappointment-1844/consequ: Later influence on the Bible Student movement
events/laestadian-revival-1844/summary: Lars Levi Laestadius, Lutheran pastor and botanist at Karesuando in Swedish Lapland, experienced a spiritual awakening in 1844, which he attributed to a conversation with a Sami woman, Milla Clementsdotter. His preaching sparked a revival among Sami, Finnish and Swedish people of the far north.
events/laestadian-revival-1844/causes/0: Alcohol abuse and poverty in the north
events/laestadian-revival-1844/causes/1: Earlier Pietist awakenings in the Nordic countries
events/laestadian-revival-1844/consequen: Laestadian movement within the Nordic Lutheran churches
Emigration of Laestadians to North America and later divisions into several branches
events/southern-baptist-convention-1845/: Founding of the Southern Baptist Convention at Augusta

In May 1845 Baptists from the slaveholding states met in Augusta, Georgia, and formed the Southern Baptist Convention after the national Baptist mission bodies refused to appoint slaveholders as missionaries. The split was over slavery: Southern delegates defended the right of slaveholders to serve, and the new convention's founders included many enslavers. The SBC formally repudiated this history in a 1995 resolution on racial reconciliation, apologising to African Americans and acknowledging that the convention had been founded in part to defend slavery.
The Home Mission Society declined in 1844 to appoint the Georgia slaveholder James E. Reeve as a missionary (a deliberate test case)
The Boston-based foreign mission board's reply to the 'Alabama Resolutions' that it would not appoint a slaveholder
Sectional tensions that also split the Methodists (1844) and Presbyterians
Creation of what became the largest Protestant denomination in the United States
Northern Baptists continued in the older societies, organising as the Northern Baptist Convention in 1907
Freed Black Baptists formed their own conventions after emancipation
1995 SBC resolution repenting of the convention's defence of slavery and racism
events/lcms-founded-1847/summary: German Lutheran pastors, including Saxon immigrants led by C. F. W. Walther and missionaries sent by Wilhelm Löhe, organised 'The German Evangelical Lutheran Synod of Missouri, Ohio, and Other States' at Chicago in April 1847.
events/lcms-founded-1847/causes/0: Saxon emigration of 1838–39 seeking confessional freedom
events/lcms-founded-1847/causes/1: Opposition to the Prussian Union and to 'American Lutheranism'
events/lcms-founded-1847/consequences/1: Network of parochial schools and Concordia seminaries
events/bethesda-controversy-1848/title: The Bethesda controversy divides the Brethren
events/bethesda-controversy-1848/summary: When Bethesda Chapel in Bristol, led by George Müller and Henry Craik, received worshippers from B. W. Newton's Plymouth assembly — whose Christological teaching John Nelson Darby had condemned — Darby issued a circular in August 1848 calling for assemblies to refuse fellowship with Bethesda. The Brethren divided into 'Exclusive' assemblies, which held that a decision binds all connected meetings, and 'Open' assemblies, which treat each local assembly as autonomous.
events/bethesda-controversy-1848/causes/: Dispute over B. W. Newton's teaching on Christ's sufferings
Competing views of church discipline and the unity of assemblies
Personal tensions between leading Brethren teachers
events/bethesda-controversy-1848/consequ: Permanent separation of Open and Exclusive Brethren
Further Exclusive divisions (1881, 1890 Raven, and later the Taylor-led Plymouth Brethren Christian Church)
Open Brethren became a major missionary movement in Africa, India and Latin America
events/taiping-rebellion-1851/summary: Hong Xiuquan, after reading a Protestant tract and visionary experiences, proclaimed himself Jesus' younger brother and led the 'Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace' from Nanjing. The civil war cost perhaps 20 million lives and left lasting Chinese suspicion of Christianity as subversive.
events/agra-debate-1854/title: Agra debate between Pfander and Kairanawi
events/agra-debate-1854/summary: In April 1854 the CMS missionary Karl Pfander and Thomas Valpy French publicly debated the Muslim scholar Rahmatullah Kairanawi and Dr Wazir Khan at Agra on the corruption (tahrif) of the Bible and the Trinity. Kairanawi deployed European higher criticism against the missionaries, and the debate was widely regarded in India as a Muslim victory.
events/agra-debate-1854/causes/0: Evangelical missionary expansion in British India
events/agra-debate-1854/consequences/0: Kairanawi’s Izhar al-Haqq (1864) became a standard Muslim polemic against the Bible
events/agra-debate-1854/consequences/1: Highlighted the impact of biblical criticism on interreligious apologetics
events/immaculate-conception-dogma-1854/: In the bull Ineffabilis Deus (8 December 1854), Pius IX defined that Mary was preserved from original sin from the first moment of her conception by a singular grace in view of Christ's merits. It was the first dogma proclaimed by a pope on his own authority after consulting bishops.
Long-standing devotion and Franciscan theology (Duns Scotus)
events/niger-mission-onitsha-1857/summar: Samuel Ajayi Crowther founded the CMS Niger Mission with an all-African staff at Onitsha. Consecrated bishop in Canterbury Cathedral in 1864, he became the first African Anglican bishop; European missionaries later undermined him, and his forced resignation (1890) prompted African church independence movements.
events/niger-mission-onitsha-1857/conseq: African independent churches after Crowther's humiliation
events/crc-secession-1857/title: Secession of 1857 and the Christian Reformed Church
events/crc-secession-1857/summary: In 1857 several congregations of Dutch immigrants in west Michigan left the Reformed Protestant Dutch Church (today's Reformed Church in America), objecting to its Americanised practices such as hymn singing, open communion and tolerance of Freemasonry. They formed what became the Christian Reformed Church.
events/crc-secession-1857/causes/0: Heritage of the 1834 Afscheiding (Secession) in the Netherlands
events/crc-secession-1857/causes/1: Suspicion of American revivalism and lodge membership
events/crc-secession-1857/consequences/0: Christian Reformed Church in North America
events/origin-of-species-1859/title: Publication of On the Origin of Species
events/origin-of-species-1859/summary: Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species on 24 November 1859, arguing for common descent through natural selection. Christian responses ranged from enthusiastic accommodation (Asa Gray, Charles Kingsley, later B. B. Warfield) to sharp rejection of its apparent exclusion of design (Charles Hodge).
events/origin-of-species-1859/consequenc: Undermined Paley-style design arguments from biological adaptation
Sharpened debates over Genesis, human origins and theodicy
Eventually provoked organised anti-evolution movements in the 20th century
events/free-methodist-church-1860/title: Founding of the Free Methodist Church at Pekin
events/free-methodist-church-1860/summar: After B. T. Roberts and other 'Nazarite' preachers were expelled from the Genesee Conference of the Methodist Episcopal Church for criticising its worldliness, laity and ministers met at Pekin, New York, in August 1860 and organised the Free Methodist Church.
events/free-methodist-church-1860/causes: Expulsion of Roberts (1858) for his critique of declining Methodist discipline
Opposition to rented pews, slaveholding and secret societies
events/free-methodist-church-1860/conseq: 'Free' seats for the poor, freedom from slavery, and freedom in worship became the church's watchwords
Early advocacy (Roberts's Ordaining Women, 1891) for women in ministry
events/reorganization-amboy-1860/title: Joseph Smith III accepts leadership of the Reorganized Church at Amboy
events/reorganization-amboy-1860/summary: On 6 April 1860 at Amboy, Illinois, Joseph Smith III, son of the Latter Day Saint founder, accepted the presidency of the 'New Organization' of Saints who had rejected Brigham Young's leadership and plural marriage. The body became the Reorganized Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, renamed Community of Christ in 2001.
events/reorganization-amboy-1860/causes/: Succession crisis after Joseph Smith's death in 1844
Rejection of Brigham Young's leadership and of polygamy
Belief in lineal succession of the prophetic office
events/reorganization-amboy-1860/consequ: Largest Latter Day Saint body after the Utah church
Later moved toward mainstream Protestant theology, ordaining women from 1984
